doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

chapter: Staying in Rome and best and worst gigs
title: Why he stayed in Rome rather than moving to New York
summary: After the Rawls years he came home when Jill was pregnant, found plenty of work and values the variety of gigs possible in a smaller market.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Did you ever consider moving somewhere else, from Rome?

Yeah I wanted to move to New York. And at the end of the Lou Rawls days I probably should have stayed out in Las Vegas or in LA, and I had a lot of opportunities to do things, but you know, I was married and then Jill got pregnant and I came home and made a go of it here.

It was a little frustrating at first, but there’s great musicians here just like anywhere else. Maybe not as many, but I still had my sights on going to New York, but I never felt like I was quite up to it in those days. I didn’t feel — I needed a little more work. I needed to get better before I go there. And then I got so entrenched here, I got so much work, I was fortunate I got so much work, why would I leave?
My friend Jimmy Wormworth would say “you’ve got to come, you could work three to four nights a week here.” I’m working six and seven nights here.
You know how many times I’m working Saturday? Come on.
Yeah I’ve got four gigs Saturday, and a Sunday brunch. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -20-

That’s one of the things probably about this area, you do get a chance to do a variety of things that maybe you wouldn’t at a bigger — like a New York setting. You know, because right away you get kind of put into a niche and even if you’re a jazz player, are you a straight ahead player, are you a modern guy, are you traditional? They have all these little sub-niches within the niche. And here you can play with the Syracuse Symphony one day, go play a show at the casino, go play a jazz gig, play a solo gig, you know a dance thing, whatever. So I think you get afforded sometimes, some opportunities that you’d be shut out of in a bigger, more competitive market.
